FINAL WAGE PAYMENT / WAITING-TIME PENALTY DEMAND LETTER
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme, Inc.

DEMAND FOR PAYMENT OF FINAL WAGES AND WAITING-TIME PENALTY
Re: Demand for Payment of Final Wages — Jordan Alex Lee

To Acme, Inc.:

This letter concerns the employment of Jordan Alex Lee, whose employment with Acme, Inc. ended on August 15, 2026. The separation is described here as: Discharged (involuntary termination).

California Labor Code sections 201 and 202 set deadlines for paying an employee's final wages depending on how the employment ended. As of the date of this letter, Jordan Alex Lee has not received full payment of final wages owed, including all earned and unpaid wages and any accrued, unused vacation or paid time off required to be paid out as wages at termination. The unpaid amount is currently identified as approximately $3,200.00.

Because final wages were not paid by the applicable statutory deadline, California Labor Code section 203 provides that unpaid wages continue as a penalty at Jordan Alex Lee's daily rate of pay — $200.00 per day — for each day payment remains outstanding, up to a maximum of 30 days.

Payment in full of the unpaid final wages described above, together with all waiting-time penalties accrued as of the date payment is made, is demanded.

WHEN FINAL WAGES BECOME DUE UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW
California law sets a specific deadline for paying an employee's final wages, and which deadline applies depends on how the employment ended. If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately. If an employee quits without giving the employer at least 72 hours' notice, final wages are due within 72 hours of the quit; if the employee gives at least 72 hours' notice, final wages are due at the time of quitting. This letter treats August 15, 2026 as the date Jordan Alex Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ended, based on a separation described here as: Discharged (involuntary termination).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 201(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.)
  "If an employee not having a written contract for a definite period quits his or her employment, his or her wages shall become due and payable not later than 72 hours thereafter, unless the employee has given 72 hours previous notice of his or her intention to quit, in which case the employee is entitled to his or her wages at the time of quitting."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 202(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=202.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when final wages become due on a discharge or a quit — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation. These are the general discharge-and-quit deadlines (Labor Code sections 201(a) and 202(a)); California law contains additional, narrower deadlines for other circumstances not addressed here (for example, a longer same-day-equivalent window for certain seasonal employees in the perishable-food industry, and separate provisions that apply only to state-government employers). Which deadline actually governed this particular separation, and whether the separation is correctly characterized as a discharge or a quit with or without notice, are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

THE WAITING-TIME PENALTY: HOW IT ACCRUES AND ITS CAP
When an employer willfully fails to pay final wages on time, California law imposes a separate penalty on top of the unpaid wages themselves. Under this rule, wages continue to accrue as a penalty at the same daily rate of pay, starting from the original due date, until they are paid in full or until a lawsuit to collect them is filed — whichever happens first. That penalty cannot exceed 30 days of wages. An employee who deliberately avoids payment, or who refuses a payment that is fully and properly offered (including any penalty already accrued), is not entitled to a penalty for the period during which they did so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days. An employee who secretes or absents themselves to avoid payment to them, or who refuses to receive the payment when fully tendered to them, including any penalty then accrued under this section, is not entitled to any benefit under this section for the time during which the employee so avoids payment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a waiting-time penalty accrues and is capped — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid-wage dispute. This penalty requires that the employer's failure to pay be ‘willful,’ a legal standard with its own body of case law addressed in a separate clause; an employer whose failure to pay was not willful is not liable under this section even if wages were, in fact, paid late. This clause states the general accrual and cap rule; it does not work through how the daily rate is calculated for pay that is not a fixed daily wage (for example, commission-based or highly variable pay). This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 203(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT “WILLFUL” MEANS FOR THE WAITING-TIME PENALTY
The waiting-time penalty does not apply automatically just because final wages were paid late — it applies only if the employer's failure to pay was “willful.” California courts have held that this does not require proof that the employer deliberately set out to cheat the employee out of money it knew was owed. It means only that the employer intentionally failed or refused to do an act that was legally required, as opposed to a failure caused by something genuinely outside the employer's control. Courts have also recognized that when an employer has a genuine, good-faith dispute about whether it is legally required to pay the wages at issue, that good-faith dispute can defeat a finding of willfulness — even if the employer later turns out to be wrong about the underlying legal question.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "As used in section 203, “willful” merely means that the employer intentionally failed or refused to perform an act which was required to be done. (Davis v. Morris (1940) 37 Cal.App.2d 269, 274 [99 P.2d 345].)"
  — Barnhill v. Robert Saunders & Co., 125 Cal. App. 3d 1 (1981) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2113705/barnhill-v-robert-saunders-co/)
  "We conclude that given that uncertainty, appellant should not be penalized for believing that setoff was proper and payment of wages not required. Accordingly, appellant's attempt to exercise a right to setoff was not wilful nonpayment of wages within the meaning of Labor Code section 203, and the imposition of penalties was inappropriate."
  — Barnhill v. Robert Saunders & Co., 125 Cal. App. 3d 1, 8-9 (1981) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2113705/barnhill-v-robert-saunders-co/)
  Known gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how ‘willful’ has been interpreted for this specific penalty — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular dispute, and not a claim that any dispute an employer raises will succeed in defeating the penalty. Both quotations below come from the same California Court of Appeal decision (which in turn quotes a still-earlier appellate decision for the core definition of ‘willful’); this research session's case-law lookups were rate-limited, and no independent second case was verified for this specific point — that gap is disclosed here rather than papered over. It's also worth being precise about what the cited case actually decided: the good-faith defense that succeeded there involved a good-faith dispute over the employer's legal right to a wage setoff, and the court was explicit that there was no dispute about the amount of wages owed. Whether a good-faith factual dispute over the amount owed would be treated the same way is a related but distinct question this clause does not resolve; the same opinion notes, without deciding, that some other jurisdictions have recognized a defense along those lines.

THE FILING DEADLINE FOR A WAITING-TIME PENALTY CLAIM
California's waiting-time penalty statute does not set its own fixed, standalone number of years within which a claim for the penalty must be filed. Instead, it ties the filing deadline for the penalty to whatever statute of limitations applies to the underlying unpaid-wage claim the penalty is based on: a lawsuit for waiting-time penalties may be filed at any time before that underlying wage claim's own statute of limitations runs out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 203(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how the filing deadline for a waiting-time-penalty claim is structured — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular claim, and not a claim about exactly how many years apply here. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 203(b)); this research session's CourtListener case-law lookups were rate-limited at the point this clause's authority was being verified, so no case law interpreting or applying this cross-reference (for example, on which limitations period applies to the underlying wage claim once it has already been paid) was independently verified, and that gap is disclosed here rather than assumed away. Figuring out the actual filing deadline requires first identifying the limitations period that applies to the underlying wage claim itself — which under California law can differ depending on how that claim is legally characterized — and that threshold question is not answered by this clause.

ACCRUED VACATION AND PTO AS PART OF FINAL WAGES
Where California's rule that vested, unused vacation or PTO must be paid out as wages at termination applies, that payout is treated as part of the final wages covered by the deadlines and the waiting-time penalty described in this letter — not as a separate category of pay with its own separate due date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=227.3)
  Known gap: This is one state's rule, used as real evidence that accrued vacation/PTO payout is legally treated as final wages — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payout, and not a claim that any particular accrued balance is actually owed here. This clause deliberately does not re-derive the underlying vacation/PTO payout rule or its authority (California Labor Code section 227.3 and the case law interpreting it) because this document set already contains a dedicated, separately verified clause covering that rule in full, including its own citations and its own disclosed limits (for example, the distinction between a no-forfeiture rule and a permissible accrual cap). This clause exists only to connect that already-covered rule to the waiting-time-penalty mechanics described elsewhere in this letter. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 227.3); no additional independent source was found for this.

CLOSING, RESERVATION OF RIGHTS, AND SIGNATURE
Please direct payment, and any response to this letter, to Jordan Alex Lee at the address below.

If full payment — including all waiting-time penalties accrued under California Labor Code section 203 — is not received, Jordan Alex Lee reserves all rights and remedies available under California law, including further accrual of statutory penalties up to the applicable cap, and any other remedy available for unpaid final wages.

Sincerely,

Jordan Alex Lee
Date: _______________
